source.title: Uncovering Logit Suppression Vulnerabilities in LLM Safety Alignment
source.authors: Yu-Xi Li; Yi Liu; Yuekang Li; Ling Shi; Ge-Lei Deng; Sheng Chen; Kai-Long Wang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present, though some figure text is garbled.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether affirmative prefixes and inference-time logit manipulation raise harmful-response rates, using methods distinct from the fine-tuning and token-KL measurements in the claim’s original sources.
record.gate_note: The study tests affirmative prompt prefixes and logit manipulation, not fine-tuning on harmful or benign datasets, per-token KL divergence, safety localization in weights, or training methods intended to deepen safety. It also evaluates several jailbreak baselines. Table 6 reports a logit-manipulation ablation, but those rows are omitted under the 60-row limit; see rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: Table 1 (JailbreakBench, five models) measures harmful-content rates with a 'Sure!' or complete affirmative prefix added to the prompt. Table 4 reports ASR for suffix and logit-manipulation attacks, and Table 5 reports ASR under defenses. These bear on V4: getting past the opening bypasses refusal. Nothing else in the claim is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paper's own conclusion is that safety alignment works by suppressing the logits of harmful content rather than removing it, so manipulating output logits recovers harmful responses. The authors present this as evidence that alignment is fragile and that existing defenses mainly catch jailbreak prompts, not the underlying vulnerability. The record's paraphrase is broadly right.
record.recipe_differences: Inference-time logit manipulation and prompt-prefix attacks; no fine-tuning intervention or KL measurement from the claim’s original methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Affirmative-prefix length and specificity change harmful-content rates; rates differ by model. Attack success also varies by attack method and defense. The study reports that prefix length m and batch size N affect VulMine ASR and runtime.
record.code_released: The paper says code is available on GitHub, but gives no URL in the text.
record.problems: Table 1 gives point rates without uncertainty estimates. Harmfulness is automatically judged with Llama-Guard-3; the paper describes its detection as nearly 100% but does not report a confidence interval. Table 5’s prose gives a 72.56% average ASR, while the displayed per-model values average to a different figure across the three listed defenses. The table caption says three defenses although the setup describes four; PPL results are shown only in a figure, whose extracted values are not legible.
record.rows_left_out: Table 6 ablation results (VulMine, VulMine-k, VulMine-m, and question-only ASR for five models) are omitted under the 60-row cap after retaining the prompt-prefix results, all Table 4 attack-by-model results, and all Table 5 defense-by-model results. Table 4 aggregate method averages and p-values are also not given separate rows. Figures 2–3 report timing and perplexity measures, not the target harmful-response behavior.

untested.parts: No test of data or objective as cause. The paper's explanation, logit suppression of affirmative tokens plus fixed refusal openers, is asserted from observation, not tested.
No deepening training. ESF (Table 5) is applied as a defense, not tested as a method that spreads safety across positions.

missing.what: Table 6 ablation: VulMine-k (initial forced affirmative tokens) vs VulMine-m (enhancement prefix) vs question-only ASR on five models. VulMine-k reaches 68.52% on average and VulMine-m 52.48%, against 4.92% question-only. This bears on whether forcing only the opening tokens is enough.
Hyperparameter sensitivity: reducing m or N substantially lowers ASR, and larger values add time but not ASR.

record.verdict_notes: This is a short ICPR paper and the experiment is a white-box attack. Harmfulness is judged only by Llama-Guard-3 and is not validated beyond a claim of nearly 100% agreement. There are no confidence intervals. Table 5's prose gives an average of 72.56% against 67-77% in the table, and the caption says three defenses while the setup lists four. P6-P15 use JailbreakBench (100 behaviours, 10 samples each) while Tables 4-5 use AdvBench (520), so the two sets are not directly comparable. The 'Sure!' text is placed at the end of the user prompt, not in the assistant turn. Under V4 only the Table 1 prompt prefixes and VulMine tests count as direct evidence. The jailbreak-baseline rows (A1-A25) are the study's reference points, not its own result.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples is performed.
No ordinary or carefully chosen benign-data fine-tuning is tested. ESF is evaluated as a defense, not as a test of benign-data erosion.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement is reported.

Tests affirmative input prefixes and logit-manipulation attacks, including one suffix-mode baseline. Does not test decoding changes; does not isolate whether simply prefilling a few compliant tokens is sufficient from the other prompt changes in its complete-prefix condition.
No weight or rank localization is tested.
No experiment tests whether training data or the training objective causes safety shallowness.
No training that spreads safety across response positions, or evaluation of whether such training holds up, is reported.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7b-chat
rows.operation_detail: VulMine manipulates output logits to guide a harmful response.
rows.note: ASR is successful harmful-content generation divided by total harmful queries.
rows.check: VulMine forces affirmative opening tokens by raising their logits and suppressing denial tokens. This is a decoding change that bypasses refusal. ASR is 95.93%, but the study is white-box and uses a best-of-N search (N=2000), so it is not comparable to single-shot prefills.

relationships.condition: Llama-3-8b, Mistral-7b and gemma-7b, plus all five models under VulMine logit manipulation; affirmative prompt prefix on Mistral and Llama-3
relationships.reason: 'Sure!' raises Mistral from 20.5% to 58.35% (P8) and Llama-3 from 1.8% to 35.15% (P9). The complete prefix gives 76.85% and 41.55% (P13, P14). VulMine forcing the opening reaches 90-98% on all five (A26-A30).
relationships.display_finding: 'Sure!' raised Mistral from 20.5% to 58.35% and Llama-3 from 1.8% to 35.15%, the complete prefix gave 76.85% and 41.55%, and VulMine forcing of the opening reached 90–98% on all five models.

relationships.condition: Llama-2-7b/13b-chat and gemma-7b-it under the prompt-prefix variant, and VulMine under the defenses
relationships.reason: Prompt prefixes only reach 8.2-18.65% on Llama-2 and gemma (P6, P7, P10, P11, P12, P15), so an appended prefix does not bypass refusal there. Under defenses VulMine falls to 57.69-86.92% (D1-D15), well short of the undefended 90-98%.
relationships.display_finding: Prompt prefixes reached only 8.2–18.65% on Llama-2 and gemma-7b-it. Under defenses VulMine fell to 57.69–86.92%, short of its undefended 90–98%.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Affirmative prefixes on the five tested models; VulMine across the five models; suffix-mode GCG/COLD baselines where successful.
reader_labels.reason: Harmful-content rates increase with affirmative prefixes, and attack methods including logit manipulation produce harmful responses at the reported rates; see P6–P15, A1–A5, A21–A30.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Variation across models and under the evaluated defenses.
reader_labels.reason: Prefix effects are incomplete and vary substantially by model; attack rates also fall under defenses, with several below the unmitigated VulMine results; see P6–P15 and D1–D15.
